tagline.text: Baler river-mouth surf break named after an Apocalypse Now filming scene

location.label: Location
location.text: North of Sabang Beach at the Tibag-Sabang River mouth, Baler, Aurora

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800~2,000 (surfing, transport and meals, excluding lodging, per person per day)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL), about 5–7 hours by road

children.text: Charlie's Point is a surf break at the mouth of the Tibag-Sabang River, where it meets the Pacific Ocean in Baler, Aurora. It is said to take its name from a scene in the film Apocalypse Now, and it is quieter than Sabang Beach with slightly bigger waves.

Charlie's Point is the surf spot with the most stories in Baler, which is officially recognized as the birthplace of Philippine surfing. Head north from Sabang Beach and you reach the mouth where the Tibag-Sabang River flows into the sea, and here the river meets the Pacific swell and the waves break in long lines. Wikipedia explains that the cast of Apocalypse Now often surfed after filming, and the spot shown in the film came to be called Charlie's Point. The movie is set in Vietnam, but it was actually shot in Baler.

Surfing in Baler goes back to the early 1970s. The story goes that Steve Scott, an American surfer living at the Subic naval base, took his board to the east coast of Luzon in 1972 and found waves in Baler, then a remote fishing village. On August 6, 2023, Republic Act No. 11957 officially recognized Baler as the birthplace of Philippine surfing. Baler's surf spots fall roughly into beginner-friendly Sabang Beach, intermediate Cemento, Lindy's Point with its powerful waves, and Charlie's Point at the river mouth. Comparing them shows what makes Charlie's Point different. Sabang Beach has small to medium left and right waves over sand, which makes it best for beginners and novices, and surf schools and board rentals sit right on the beach. Cemento (Cobra Reef) has a coral bottom and is for experienced surfers; sea urchins are reported on the paddle-out, so reef booties are needed. Lindy's Point has tall, unpredictable waves that are not for beginners, and one account says it formed when local engineers opened the river mouth into Baler Bay for flood control. Charlie's Point sits between these, offering the long waves typical of a river mouth.

Descriptions of the waves at Charlie's Point differ from source to source. One guide calls it a long right-hander over a sandy river-mouth bottom, while a surf forecasting site classifies it as a beach break with both rights and lefts. The bottom is a mix of sand and gravel and is said to be rougher than the fine sand at Sabang. Opinions on difficulty also differ. Some say it suits all levels, others say it suits experienced surfers who want slightly bigger waves, so it is safest to assume that beginners should try it only on calm days.

When planning your trip, split your days according to how much you want to surf. If you are new to surfing, take a lesson or two at Sabang and practice standing up first, then go and watch conditions at Charlie's Point once you are comfortable with the waves. If you have experience, rent a board from your lodging for the day, head to the river mouth early in the morning, and rest at midday when the waves get messy. Sabang Beach is often crowded with students on weekends, so spending the morning at the quieter river mouth is another option. The waves and bottom change from day to day, so ask a local surfer about the conditions that day. There is also something to see for travelers who do not surf. The farther north you go from the hotel stretch, the fewer people you meet, and early in the morning it is pleasant to walk the quiet beach and watch the waves and surfers at the river mouth. This is a surf spot, not a swimming beach with lifeguards, so swim at Sabang and treat this place as somewhere to watch and take photos. Conditions change often, so check the latest information with your lodging or a surf school.

blocks.title: Waves at the Tibag-Sabang River mouth

children.text: Swell from the Pacific breaks in long lines at the mouth where the river flows out to sea. The waves are said to be cleanest on days when a north groundswell arrives. The sand at the river mouth shifts, so the shape of the waves can change from day to day.

The place where the surfing scene in the film was shot came to be called Charlie's Point. Once you know where the name comes from, an ordinary beach becomes a place with a story. You can hear film stories all around Baler town. The filming is said to have helped spread surf culture in Baler.

blocks.title: Waves one step bigger than Sabang

children.text: If Sabang Beach has medium-sized waves for beginners, this spot suits intermediate surfers who want slightly more powerful waves. On calm days the waves can be small enough for beginners to try. If you are not confident in your ability, go with an instructor.

There are far fewer people here than along the Sabang stretch with its hotels and surf schools. There are relatively few surfers too, so lineups tend to be short. In the early morning you can watch the sun rise over the river mouth.

blocks.title: A stop on the birthplace-of-surfing tour

children.text: Charlie's Point is one of the surf spots of Baler that you visit along with Sabang Beach, Lindy's Point and Cemento. Many surfers visit two or three spots in a day to compare the waves. Renting a tricycle makes getting around easy.

Just watching surfers ride long waves at the river mouth is worth the trip. The light is good in the morning and around sunset. When photographing surfers, do not get too close, and be polite and say hello.

blocks.title: Linking up with Baler surf schools

children.text: A common approach is to take lessons at a surf school on Sabang Beach and then move over to Charlie's Point on a day when conditions are good. It helps to ask your instructor which spot is best that day. Decide in advance how you will carry your board there.

Head north from Sabang Beach by tricycle or on foot. A tricycle is the easiest way if you are carrying a board, and walking takes quite a while.
When you arrive at the river mouth, first watch the waves and currents for 10–20 minutes. Check where the channel flows out to sea and where the surfers catch waves.
If you feel confident, paddle out. If you are only watching, stay on the sand at the river mouth, watch the surfers and waves, and take photos.
Return to Sabang for breakfast at a beachfront restaurant and rest.
Rest at midday when the wind shifts and the waves get messy, and then in the afternoon you can take a beginner lesson at Sabang Beach.

Charlie's Point is at the river mouth north of Sabang, and going by tricycle or motorbike is the practical choice. Some guides say walking takes about
1 hour
If you bring a board, ask the driver beforehand whether it can be carried, and negotiate the fare.

The surf season is generally given as September to March. From September to November typhoon-driven swells bring big waves, and from December to March the amihan monsoon makes waves cleaner, with size and quality at their best in December and January.
From April to August the sea is calm, which suits beginners and non-surfing travelers, but Charlie's Point may often have weak waves. Do not go into the water when a typhoon is approaching.

Most lodging is on Sabang Beach, and you get to Charlie's Point from there by tricycle. Options range from budget places and surf camps to upscale resorts, and surf camps offer board rental and lessons together. Book early for Holy Week and for Christmas and New Year. Surf camps, resorts and budget places along Sabang Beach are the usual choices, and budget lodging is reported at about ₱800~1,100 per night, so check current rates.

For meals, use the restaurants and carinderias on Sabang Beach. Beachfront restaurants cost about ₱300 per person, and carinderias are cheap but can run out of food before lunch. There are almost no restaurants around Charlie's Point, so bring water and snacks.

After surfing it is common to eat at Sabang Beach restaurants, with fish dishes, fruit drinks and grilled food. Popular restaurants can have long lines in peak season, so go a little later after you finish surfing. If you head out to surf early, it helps to ask your lodging the night before to prepare a simple breakfast.

A tricycle for the ride back from Charlie's Point can be hard to find locally, so agree on waiting or pickup time with the driver in advance.
On the day after rain, when the water is murky, avoid the river mouth and take a lesson at Sabang Beach instead.
Because this is a river mouth, dangerous rip currents can form and there are no lifeguards, so go in only at your skill level.
A surf forecasting site warns of dangerous rips here. Do not go far out alone.
River mouths have fast currents and a bottom that can change, so after rain the water is murky and dangerous.
The bottom is sand and gravel, so you can get hurt when you fall.
When a typhoon is approaching, stay out of the water and follow local announcements.
Treat a beach with no flags as having no lifeguards and do not go into the water.
